title: The Promise and Pitfalls of Land Value Taxes: How Smart Policy Design Can Advance Progressive Goals (Rita Jefferson, ITEP, 24 Nov 2026)
what_was_fetched: Full brief text, one curl request (HTTP 200, 226 KB HTML); text extracted to fetched/itep.txt (36 KB incl. 32 endnotes). Figures 1-4 are images/downloads and were not read.
verdict: ENRICH objections/homevoters-will-block-lvt.md (one attributed sentence); optional second sentence on places/pennsylvania.md for Scranton. No NEW page.
verdict_reason: A progressive think-tank's considered, cautious position (LVT 'might not be as progressive a tax as it once was'; distribution depends on parcel mix and assessment accuracy) is useful as origin-only attribution. It is a secondary synthesis of Lincoln/academic work and advocacy-group modelling, with no original analysis of its own, so it does not support a new page. It fits the regressivity theme best on objections/lvt-hurts-asset-rich-cash-poor.md (the winner/loser parcel examples) or homevoters-will-block-lvt.md (winners-and-losers backlash, Pittsburgh 2001); the Pittsburgh-reassessment backlash point fits homevoters. Choose one.
claim_grade: Tier 2 (ITEP, advocacy-research think-tank per people-tiers.json). Its design cautions and framing are D/origin-only. Its historical and empirical claims are secondhand B-claims whose primaries are Tier 1 and should be cited directly: Lincoln Institute (Dye & England 2009; Hughes 2006; Yang 2014; Anderson & Allen 2022), Oates & Schwab 1997 (NTJ), Yang & Hawley 2022 (Public Finance Review), Kentucky HB 607, Cohen & Fedele 2017. ITEP's 'recent' Pennsylvania facts (11 cities, Scranton ended 2025) rest on local newspapers (Times-Tribune; Pocono Review).
content_summary: Scope claim (Overview): 'Kentucky, Pennsylvania, and Virginia are the only states that currently allow certain municipalities to adopt split-rate property taxation.' Later contradicted in the same brief: 'Pennsylvania is the only state in the country where cities use land value taxation' (i.e. in actual use).

Framing: modern LVT is 'a form of property tax reform aimed at driving specific development patterns', not George's single tax; interest is 'more to do with land use policy than with potential revenues'. Concedes 'Compared to George's time, taxing land values might not be as progressive a tax as it once was' because low- and middle-income wealth is mostly primary residences (esp. Black and Latino families; Fed Distributional Financial Accounts Q1 2026, endnotes 5-6).

Incidence ('Are Land Value Taxes Progressive?'): revenue-neutral reform shifts burden to under-developed parcels in high-land-value areas. Two worked contrasts: investor-owned vacant lot vs adjacent apartment building (progressive, part of cut passed to renters); old small house vs new luxury build on equal land (regressive if old-home owner has lower income). Progressivity 'matched closely with the ability of assessors to determine the value of land separately' (Pennsylvania). Studies by LVT advocates on Cincinnati (Notre Dame Student Policy Network with Center for Land Economics, Apr 2026), Detroit (Anderson & Allen, Lincoln 2022) and DC (Tax Revision Commission 2025) find split rate typically lowers multifamily tax, mixed for single-family; neighborhood-matching technique.

Pennsylvania: 11 communities incl. Harrisburg use split-rate (as of Nov 2026); no mandatory reassessment schedule in state law. Pittsburgh and Scranton (both since 1913) stopped in 2001 and 2025 'due to political blowback over new assessments' (endnote 8: Times-Tribune 7 Nov 2025; Pocono Review 26 Dec 2025). Yang & Hawley 2022: largest value gains to commercial property, concentrated downtown. A 2006 study: 'an estimated 54 percent of homeowners paid more under the combined millage than they would have under split-rate' (Pittsburgh; endnote 24 cites 2018 PA Local Government Commission guide and a 2025 WESA lawsuit story, which does not look like the source of the 54% figure; locator unclear). Pittsburgh LVT spurred CBD development with limited spillover to marginalised neighbourhoods.

Virginia: 'eight of its 38 cities' authorised (incl. Richmond), none yet implemented; Virginia already requires separate land/building assessment. Progress & Policy Institute (Hoskins & Faass, Mar 2024) modelled revenue-neutral Richmond LVT as 'slightly progressive'; suggests adopting before upzoning to recapture windfall. (ITEP gives the 2024 institute name as 'Progress & Policy Institute' in the endnote and 'Progress and Poverty Institute' in the text.)

Kentucky: 'In April 2026, Kentucky passed a law allowing Louisville to use split-rate taxation' (HB 607, enrolled 14 Apr 2026); rates not yet set; advocates stressed surface parking and underused parcels. No mention of veto override, Urban Services District, revenue-neutrality, or Ordinance 8062725.

Design recommendations: articulate goals (revenue-neutral for blight vs revenue-positive for transit; 'no LVT would be right for a community that is concerned about inducing excessive development', citing Hawaii); check state uniformity clauses/constitutional amendment; build assessment capacity (land/improvement split can be inaccurate even when totals are accurate; CAMA 'often opaque'); pair with zoning reform; model parcel-level distribution before proposing; use phase-ins, exemptions, circuit breakers (cites ITEP's own 9 Nov 2026 circuit-breaker report); LVT 'cannot generate economic activity where underlying conditions for it are absent'.
Racial equity: 'one equity tool among many'; not a substitute for anti-displacement measures, CLTs, affordable housing.

History sections: Pennsylvania 1913 / 1965 Act 511 / Pittsburgh 1997 Oates-Schwab / Harrisburg 1975; Hawaii 1965-1977 (improvement rate 90% to 40% of land rate; Waikiki hotel boom; repealed by 1977; counties later reverted); Houston Pastoriza struck down under Texas uniformity clause; Amsterdam NY 1993 repealed; Connecticut 2013 pilot, no takers, Cohen & Fedele find modestly progressive but assessment inconsistencies in Hartford, New Haven, New London.

Conclusion: LVT 'can be an effective policy tool with real theoretical grounding and some empirical support, but its effectiveness depends heavily on local conditions, institutional capacity, and the specific outcomes policymakers are seeking.'
existing_wiki_coverage: ITEP is cited only for circuit breakers (places/kentucky.md source 3; concepts/property-tax-circuit-breaker.md, which says ITEP's report 'does not discuss land value taxation'; that remark is about the 9 Nov report, still true). No places/virginia.md exists. Virginia's eight cities and HB 282 are in events/2026-state-lvt-enablement-wave.md (matches ITEP's 'eight' and 'none implemented'; wiki is more detailed: names the four added cities, 1998 AG opinion, HB 282 date). Kentucky HB 607 is covered in far more detail on the enablement-wave page and places/kentucky.md (veto override, Urban Services District, revenue-neutrality, bar on land-only taxation, Ordinance 8062725). Pennsylvania/Pittsburgh coverage: places/pennsylvania.md and places/pittsburgh.md and harrisburg-pennsylvania.md cite Hughes 2006 (33 municipalities: 16 current, 5 rescinded, 12 considered), Hartzok, Daume, Oates-Schwab; Scranton's 2025 abandonment of split millage is NOT on the wiki (only Scranton's 1913 adoption); ITEP's '11 cities' count conflicts with Hughes' 16 (different dates; ITEP's is current). Regressivity is handled on objections/lvt-hurts-asset-rich-cash-poor.md (CWC modelling, England & Zhao, Plummer, Bowman & Bell) and winner/loser backlash on objections/homevoters-will-block-lvt.md; objections/lvt-invites-assessment-corruption.md covers assessment. concepts/split-rate-taxation.md mentions Pennsylvania, Cohen & Coughlin, Miller & Hoskins, no ITEP. Detroit/Anderson & Allen, Hawaii, Houston, Amsterdam NY, Connecticut are not checked here beyond Amsterdam (no Amsterdam NY hit in places/concepts).
scanner_premise_errors: 'Kentucky, Pennsylvania and Virginia (the only states authorising municipal split-rate)': accurately attributes ITEP's sentence, but it is a loose claim. It matches the wiki enablement-wave account of the three 2026 actions only if read as 'authorise now'; the wiki's own page lists New York City's IBX district as a third 2026 action and does not claim exclusivity. Lincoln/Hughes 2006 describe Pennsylvania as the sole enabling state at that date. The brief contradicts itself ('Pennsylvania is the only state in the country where cities use land value taxation'), so do not repeat the 'only three' wording as fact; if used, attribute and date it.
'The wiki already cites ITEP for circuit breakers (Tier 1/2 institution)': ITEP is Tier 2 only (people-tiers.json), not Tier 1.

'First LVT piece': plausible but the brief itself cross-references ITEP's 9 Nov 2026 circuit-breaker report as its endnote 17, so the two are related; the circuit-breaker page's 'does not discuss land value taxation' is accurate for that report.

'Vacant/underused land and speculation framing': ITEP actually leads with land-use and density rather than revenue and speculation, and says LVT 'might not be as progressive a tax as it once was'; the scanner's framing ('advance progressive goals') overstates the brief's confidence. Title promises design for progressive goals; body is cautious.

Not an error but a gap: scanner lists complementary land-use policy among 'design considerations'; ITEP also lists goal-setting, parcel-level distributional modelling and racial equity, and history sections on Hawaii, Houston, Amsterdam NY, Connecticut that the scanner omits.
uncertainties: The '54 percent of homeowners paid more' figure (Pittsburgh, 2006 study) is not traceable to a named study in the endnotes; do not carry it. Endnote numbering in the extract appears offset by one in the history section (e.g. note 25 is a Joni Mitchell/Waikiki citation placed after a Pennsylvania reassessment sentence), so locators for footnoted claims are approximate. ITEP's 'Pittsburgh and Scranton... stopped 2001 and 2025' rests on local news; Scranton's end of split millage should be verified from a primary (Scranton 2026 budget ordinance) before entering any page. ITEP says 11 PA cities use split-rate; Lincoln/Hughes counted 16 earlier; counts differ by date and definition. Figures not read.
suggested_text: The Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a progressive tax-policy think-tank, argues that a revenue-neutral land value tax can be progressive or regressive depending on the mix of parcels (a tax cut for a large apartment building against an increase for an underbuilt investor-owned lot would be progressive; an increase on an older modest home against a cut for an adjacent new luxury home would not be), and that outcomes track how accurately assessors separate land from improvements; it points to the political reaction to Pittsburgh's 2001 reassessment as an example, and recommends parcel-level distributional modelling, phase-ins and circuit breakers before adoption (ITEP, November 2026; a think-tank's policy position, not an empirical finding).

title: Pricing the Value of Land: Ground Rent and the System of Housing Land Provision in Australia (Joe Collins, Preprints.org, posted 18 Nov 2026)
what_was_fetched: doi.org request redirected to preprints.org and returned 403 Access Denied (one attempt, no retry). One Crossref API request succeeded: metadata plus full abstract (posted-content, preprint, MDPI AG, accepted 17 Nov 2026, CC BY 4.0, 0 references deposited, no author affiliation deposited, no ORCID). Full text not read. Saved as fetched/collins_cr.json and fetched/collins.html (the 403 page).
verdict_reason: Only the abstract is readable; full text, method detail and affiliation are unavailable. The editorial rule allows at most one attributed sentence for an unrefereed preprint 'only if the text is readable'. An abstract alone supports no more than a pointer, and the author's identity is unverified. Re-check when a publisher PDF or journal version appears.
claim_grade: D (unrefereed preprint; Tier 2 by rubric: author unidentified, venue is a preprint server, abstract-only). The one empirical claim in the abstract (residential land values rose nineteen-fold 1990-2025 while dwelling completions were 'little changed') is a B-claim that must be traced to national accounts/ABS series before use; the abstract names the source types (national accounts, valuers-general, central bank, tax authorities) but no figures.
content_summary: Argument (abstract): standard valuation methods, 'hedonic pricing, mass appraisal and spatial econometrics treat housing land as a bundle of locational, structural and amenity attributes wherein price is set at market equilibrium, and in so doing they take the social relations of production giving rise to land prices as given.'

Alternative: map housing-land provision 'as an interlocking, dynamic system of social relations, from production through distribution and exchange to consumption', applying 'a theory of capitalist landed property'. The vocabulary (production/distribution/exchange/consumption, capitalist landed property, forms of ground rent) points to a Marxian political-economy lineage (Marx on ground rent; probably Harvey/Haila-type urban rent theory), but the abstract names no authors and the reference list is not deposited, so lineage is inference only.

Method: because official statistics are compiled in price rather than value categories, it 'triangulates price series from the national accounts, valuers-general, the central bank and the tax authorities as proxies for the forms of ground rent.'

Empirical: Australia case study; residential land values rose 19-fold between 1990 and 2025 while annual dwelling completions were little changed; ground rent is shared among landowners, lenders and the state. Closes on implications for land-market regulation, equity and spatial justice.

Note: the scanner's 'proposes a ground-rent-based valuation' is a stretch; the abstract describes a system-mapping and triangulation approach for analysing ground rent, not a replacement valuation formula for assessors.
existing_wiki_coverage: concepts/ground-rent.md (economic definition, distinguishes legal ground rent), concepts/mass-appraisal-methods.md (hedonic regression section; no critique from Marxian rent theory), concepts/residual-land-valuation.md, places/australia.md. No Joe Collins anywhere on the wiki; 'Collins' hits are Josh Ryan-Collins, Toby Lloyd and Laurie Macfarlane (Rethinking the Economics of Land and Housing; places/netherlands.md), a different author with a different, peer-reviewed/book-length line of work. The abstract's three-way split of ground rent among landowners, lenders and the state parallels Ryan-Collins's 'land and mortgage credit' argument, which is likely why a mix-up is tempting; do not conflate.
scanner_premise_errors: Scanner says the paper 'proposes ground-rent-based valuation for the Australian housing land provision system': the abstract does not say that; it proposes a relational, system-of-provision mapping and a proxy-triangulation method and closes by 'setting out what such an approach offers' for regulation and equity.

Scanner's 'on-topic for ground-rent and housing-affordability pages' is fair, but 'hedonic ... miss ground rent' is the scanner's paraphrase; the abstract's actual complaint is that they take the social relations behind land prices as given.
'Landing page 403 bot-walled from this environment but live': confirmed (403 Access Denied via Akamai); the DOI also resolves in Crossref, so the record is real.
uncertainties: Author identity and affiliation not confirmed (Crossref carries no affiliation or ORCID); no basis to say whether he is the Western Sydney political economist the brief asked about, so do not state an affiliation on any page. Whether the paper engages Georgist theory, Haila, Harvey or Marx explicitly is unknown. The 19-fold figure's basis (nominal? residential land only? ABS 'Total value of dwellings: land component'?) is unknown; ABS national balance-sheet data would be the primary to check independently. Whether a journal version follows is unknown.

title: 'Sunlight and Wind Pension': Just Energy Transition and Common Wealth Basic Income (Nam Hoon Kang, Basic Income Studies, online 20 Nov 2026)
what_was_fetched: doi.org returned HTTP 202 with an empty body (one attempt, no retry). One Crossref API request succeeded: full metadata and abstract, journal-article, author affiliation deposited as 'Emeritus Professor, Department of Economics and Finance, Hanshin University, Osan-si, South Korea', 16 references deposited. Full text not read (paywalled/shell). Saved as fetched/kang_cr.json.
verdict: ENRICH places/south-korea.md (add the journal article beside the BIEN 2024 presentation as source 6; keep source 5; add one clause to the body sentence)
verdict_reason: Peer-reviewed, same author, same 'common wealth rent / common wealth basic income' framing, and it extends the page's Korean basic-income thread to the Lee government's 'Sunlight and Wind Pension'. It should be added, not substituted: the page's source 5 note rests on the presentation PDF read in full (Shinan example, funding-from-rents argument), and the Shinan example cannot be verified in the journal article from the abstract. Only the abstract was read, so claims must stay within it.
claim_grade: B/C (peer-reviewed journal, Tier 1 as a scholarly venue; but author is an advocate-scholar within the Basic Income Korea Network, and the argument is theoretical/normative (C/D-claim), not empirical). The abstract's statements that 'carbon rent' wanes and 'renewable energy rent grows significantly over time' are the author's theoretical claims, attributed. The characterisation of the pension as a policy 'proposed by President Lee Jae-myung' is an A-claim needing a primary (Lee campaign/government document) or news source, not Kang.
content_summary: Abstract: 'This paper examines the theoretical underpinnings of the "Sunlight and Wind Pension", a basic income policy proposed by South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to facilitate a just energy transition.'

'The progression of energy transition gives rise to two forms of economic rent: carbon rent and renewable energy rent.' Carbon rent 'is substantial but wanes in subsequent stages, whereas renewable energy rent grows significantly over time.'

Because the rents 'originate from the natural and social common wealth, their redistribution as basic income is theoretically justified.' Carbon dividends capture carbon rent; the Sunlight and Wind Pension 'aims to capture renewable energy rent'; both are 'critical components for ensuring the energy transition does not exacerbate inequality as it matures.'

Reference list (Crossref, 16 refs) includes Boyce, The Case for Carbon Dividends (Polity 2019) and a RAND report (10.7249/P2488-1), an Ecological Economics 2018 article (10.1016/j.ecolecon.2018.03.030), i.e. the carbon-dividend literature, consistent with the abstract. Not otherwise examined.
existing_wiki_coverage: places/south-korea.md line 28: 'the Basic Income Korean Network's "common wealth rent" framing (Kang, BIEN Congress 2024) argues dividends should be financed from land and commons rents rather than general taxation ... [5]'. Source 5 (line 81): Kang, 'Common Wealth Rent and Common Wealth Basic Income', BIEN Congress 2024 presentation, PDF read in full 2026-07-18; Shinan County sunshine-pension ($400/resident from solar-farm land rent) appears ONLY in the source-5 note, not in the body text. Lee Jae-myung's land-dividend proposal is in the same paragraph; the 'Sunlight and Wind Pension' is not mentioned. concepts/citizens-dividend.md and concepts/resource-rents.md have no hits for Kang, Shinan, sunshine/sunlight, 'common wealth basic income', carbon rent or renewable energy rent; narratives/ecological-rent.md and research/barnes-sky-trust.md cover carbon dividends (Boyce, Barnes). Candidate homes for a one-line cross-link: concepts/resource-rents.md (renewable-energy rent as a new rent category) and narratives/ecological-rent.md.
scanner_premise_errors: Scanner says 'journal version of the same author's BIEN 2024 presentation (same Shinan example)': the abstract does not mention Shinan, and the article is not shown to be a version of the presentation; its subject is the Sunlight and Wind Pension and carbon dividends, whereas the presentation (per the wiki's note) was a general funding-from-common-wealth-rent argument. Treat it as a related later paper, not a confirmed journal version.

Scanner says 'basic income funded by carbon rent and renewable energy rent': accurate to the abstract, but the abstract frames carbon dividends and the Sunlight and Wind Pension as distinct instruments (the first captures carbon rent, the second renewable energy rent), and says carbon rent declines over time.

Scanner implies the article should replace the presentation citation: the existing source 5 supports claims (Shinan example, rent-based financing) that the article's abstract cannot confirm; add beside, do not replace.

Existing page error to fix regardless: the body sentence calls it 'the Basic Income Korean Network's ... framing (Kang ...)' while source 5 describes Kang as 'Hanshin University, Korea Inequality Research Lab'; Crossref now shows him as Emeritus Professor, Hanshin University. Check the BIKN attribution in the presentation PDF before editing.
uncertainties: Only the abstract was read; the Shinan example, the Lee government's actual funding design and any land-rent content cannot be checked. Whether 'common wealth basic income' in the article extends to land rent (as in the presentation) is unknown, so the body sentence should not be widened to say the article covers land. Whether 'Sunlight and Wind Pension' is in fact Lee's enacted or proposed policy needs a primary/news source. Crossref's 'online 20 Nov 2026' is the publication date; volume/issue not yet assigned.
suggested_text: Kang, an emeritus economist at Hanshin University, extends the common-wealth-rent argument to energy: he treats carbon rent and renewable-energy rent as rents arising from natural and social common wealth, and argues that carbon dividends and President Lee Jae-myung's proposed 'Sunlight and Wind Pension' are the corresponding means of returning them as basic income (Basic Income Studies, 2026; a theoretical argument by an advocate-scholar, peer-reviewed). Suggested source 6: Nam Hoon Kang (2026), "'Sunlight and Wind Pension': Just Energy Transition and Common Wealth Basic Income," Basic Income Studies, online 20 November 2026, doi:10.1515/bis-2025-0016 (abstract and reference list via Crossref; full text not accessed).
